Spoken core (30-sec icebreaker): Good morning everyone. Before we begin, I want to set expectations honestly—mostly to take the pressure off myself. I am not a computer scientist or an AI specialist; I am a PhD student in ecotoxicology trained in classical statistics and mechanistic modelling. My goal today is not to lecture from above, but to share a structured, critical compass from the FRB-CESAB training I attended thanks to FR BioEEnViS.

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
The CESAB Experience
All four modules converge on a single pedagogical objective:












Official Course Objective — ai-ecol.github.io “Give participants the autonomy to assess which algorithms are most adapted to their own research questions, where to find them, and how to adjust them to the desired question.”




Spoken core (30 sec — intentional visual breather): Pause for two seconds on the word autonomy. The course was not about teaching us how to code the trendiest neural network; it was about knowing when an algorithm fits your scientific question—and when it does not.
Callback: Converges the four modules from Slide 4 into one guiding principle.
Bridge: Here is how I translated that objective into four core insights that form our roadmap for today.

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
The CESAB Experience

Autonomy to assess which algorithms fit your research question (ai-ecol.github.io) \(\rightarrow\) Translated into 4 Core Insights (Today’s Roadmap)




Insight 1 · AI > Generative Chatbots Section 1: Distinguish GenAI from the wider AI taxonomy (ML, DL, Symbolic AI) and examine cognitive & material guardrails.


Insight 2 · Domain Baseline Primes Section 2: Your scientific (e.g., ecological) knowledge anchors plausibility and dictates how a problem is framed.




Insight 3 · Exhaust Traditional Methods Section 2: Verify dimensionality and exhaust classical statistical analyses as a first step.


Insight 4 · Explicit Trade-Offs Section 3: Balance predictive gain against explainability based on the scientific goal.





Note: This session is a curated synthesis of CESAB Day 1 principles — not a 5-day syllabus dump. Session 2 (10:45 a.m.) shows how these insights landed in my PhD.

(Click 2) Section 2 combines Insights 2 and 3—your domain baseline and exhausting classical methods before scaling up. (Click 3) Section 3 addresses Insight 4—the prediction vs. explainability trade-off. (Click 4) Clarify that Part 1 is a curated conceptual compass, while Session 2 at 10:45 applies it directly to my PhD.

text:
AI Is an Umbrella Term — Not a Monolith
Quick Poll (Slido 2): Which of these four diagrams correctly organises Artificial Intelligence?





AA. Nested Algorithms







BB. AI / ML / DL / NLP / LLM









CC. AI / Data Science / Big Data







DD. CS / AI / Data Science / Math










Slido 2 — Code: #3791 5273




Answer: All four are partial lenses. There is no single formal definition of AI—each diagram highlights a different disciplinary cut (algorithms, language, data, or math).





Spoken core: Switch tab to Slido Poll 2 (Multiple Choice, ~1 min). Ask participants to pick A, B, C, or D. Once votes come in, return and click to reveal the teal box: all four are partial lenses—as CESAB Day 1 emphasized, there is no single formal consensus definition of AI.

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
Navigating the AI Vocabulary
In practice, researchers encounter a scattered soup of overlapping terms and tools:


Linear & Logistic Regression ChatGPT / Claude / Perplexity Symbolic Logic & Rules PCA / UMAP CNN & RNN Data Science & Statistics Random Forest & Decision Trees Intelligent Robots Neural Networks (MLP) Support Vector Machines (SVM) Knowledge Representation


Which field contains which—and where do everyday chatbots actually sit?



Spoken core (20 sec): When you start reading AI literature as a domain researcher, you run straight into this wall of overlapping terms—regressions, PCA, random forests, CNNs, symbolic rules, and chatbots all thrown into the same conversation.
Callback: Connects the four messy Venn diagrams on Slide 8 to the concrete tools researchers encounter.
Bridge: Let’s sort these pills into their actual nested structure.

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
Navigating the AI Vocabulary
Organizing the umbrella into parallel domains and nested subsets:

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (Umbrella Discipline)



Symbolic AI, Reasoning & Embodied Systems

Symbolic Logic & Rules Knowledge Representation Intelligent Robots


Explicit rules, ontologies, and constraint solving (e.g., protected-area design in CESAB Day 5).


Overlapping Quantitative Pillar Data Science & Statistics





MACHINE LEARNING (Automated Learning from Data)

Linear & Logistic Regression PCA / UMAP Support Vector Machines (SVM) Random Forest & Decision Trees


DEEP LEARNING (Multi-Layer Neural Networks)

Neural Networks (MLP) CNN & RNN


GENERATIVE AI & LLMs (A small, highly visible subset) ChatGPT / Claude / Perplexity







Standard reference taxonomy: The OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems classifies systems by model type (symbolic, statistical, or hybrid), learning paradigm, and transparency.



Spoken core: Point directly to the small red box at the bottom right (GenAI / LLMs). Reconnect explicitly to Slide 2’s word cloud: GenAI dominates our mental picture not because it is all of AI, but because of accessibility—anyone can ask a chatbot for a dinner recipe, whereas very few people will train a CNN or build a constraint solver. Be candid: AI capabilities are advancing rapidly and producing real scientific breakthroughs (like AlphaFold), so denying its utility makes no sense.
Callback: Closes the loop on Slide 2’s word cloud bias and sets up the taxonomy needed to understand where neural networks and LLMs live.
Bridge: And this leads directly to a personal misconception—and a paradox—that hit close to home for me when I began learning these methods…

title: Let's Talk About AI
section: My Initial Misconception & The Bio-Inspired Paradox
text:
My Initial Misconception & The Bio-Inspired Paradox
When I started learning ML, I assumed neural networks worked like my brain processing thoughts.

Inspired by biology — not biologically grounded (like a movie “based on true events”)





Biological Brain

~20 W power budget; slow electrochemical ionic spikes.
Diverse chemical neurotransmitters & local synaptic plasticity.
Learns flexibly and generalizes from few exposures.



[IMAGE: Biological Brain / Synaptic Network] Save file as: assets/images/bio_brain_network.png 






Artificial Neural Networks

Matrix multiplications over floating-point weights.
Global backpropagation optimizing a mathematical loss function.
Requires massive datasets and computational energy.



[IMAGE: Artificial Neural Network / Perceptron Layers] Save file as: assets/images/ann_perceptron_layers.png 





The Paradox: Tools loosely inspired by human cognition are increasingly used in ways that short-circuit the very biological process our brains need to learn.


Conceptual inspiration: A. Andalman (The Deep View, 2025) · C. Simon (AI Neuro Insight, 2025) · A. Karpathy (Dwarkesh Clips, 2025) · AlphaFold (Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2024)



Spoken core (3 clicks):

Initial state: Open honestly with my own misconception—coming from biology, I initially assumed artificial neural networks processed thoughts the way our brain does. In reality, ANNs are inspired by biology rather than biologically grounded, much like a movie “based on true events.”
Click 1 (Biological Brain): Our brain runs on ~20 W with slow ionic spikes, diverse chemical neurotransmitters, and local synaptic plasticity, yet learns flexibly from just a few exposures.
Click 2 (Artificial Neural Networks): ANNs rely on fast floating-point matrix multiplications, global backpropagation over a mathematical loss function, and massive compute—there are far more fundamental differences than similarities.
Click 3 (The Paradox): Ironically, tools loosely inspired by human cognition are increasingly used in ways that short-circuit the exact biological process our brains require to learn.

Callback: Connects directly to the Deep Learning & GenAI nested boxes we just mapped on Slide 10.
Bridge: Let’s look closely at how that cognitive shortcut operates in everyday scientific work.

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
Insight 1b: Cognitive Bypassing & Expertise


  
  Raw Information
  Papers · Data · Code
  
  Durable Expertise
  & Critical Audit Capacity


  
    
      
    
  
  
  
  Effortful Processing
  Cognitive Friction & Schema Building
  


  
    
      
    
  
  
  
  GenAI Shortcut — Bypasses Effortful Processing
  
  Illusion of Learning
  & Cognitive Debt






Empirical Evidence: Why Bypassing Hurts

Barcaui (2025, RCT): Lower knowledge retention when using ChatGPT as a cognitive crutch.
Gerlich (2025): Higher cognitive offloading linked to reduced critical thinking.
Kosmyna et al. (2025, arXiv preprint): Reduced EEG neural connectivity and accumulated cognitive debt. 



How LLMs Actually Operate

LLMs are probabilistic next-token generators optimized for fluency—not truth-verification engines.
Externalizing core analysis risks cognitive proletarianization (Stiegler, 2010): fluent outputs mask weak epistemic grounding and erode critical audit skills.






High Domain Background (Your Field): You form concrete hypotheses \(\rightarrow\) write precise prompts \(\rightarrow\) audit and catch errors.


Low Domain Background (Unfamiliar Field): Unclear what to ask \(\rightarrow\) vague prompts \(\rightarrow\) plausible errors go undetected.




Stiegler (2010) For a New Critique of Political Economy · Messeri & Crockett (2024) Nature 10.1038/s41586-024-07146-0 · Barcaui (2025) SSHO 10.1016/j.ssaho.2025.102287 · Gerlich (2025) Societies 10.3390/soc15010006 · Kosmyna et al. (2025) arXiv:2506.08872 (preprint) · Diagram adapted from J. Sung (2025)



Spoken core (4 clicks):

Initial state: Point to the gap between Raw Information and Durable Expertise: “To move from raw papers, data, and code to genuine expertise, one critical step is required…”
Click 1 (Teal Effortful Processing): That step is effortful processing—cognitive friction and schema building. Struggle is not a bug in learning; it is the mechanism.
Click 2 (Red GenAI Shortcut): Using GenAI to bypass that middle step does not reach expertise faster—it branches away into an illusion of learning and cognitive debt.
Click 3 (Empirical Evidence + Expertise Asymmetry): Point briefly to the empirical evidence on the left (Barcaui 2025 RCT, Gerlich 2025, Kosmyna et al. 2025 arXiv preprint), then run a 30-second rhetorical thought experiment on the right: an ecotoxicologist prompting an LLM about survival-model assumptions catches subtle flaws instantly; the same person prompting an unfamiliar metagenomics or bioinformatics pipeline gets fluent code whose hidden bugs go undetected.
Click 4 (How LLMs Actually Operate swaps into bottom-left): Explain why low-background prompting is risky—LLMs generate high-probability next tokens for fluency, not verified truth. Practical guardrail: keep cognitive friction for reasoning, writing, and analysis; delegate routine formatting or syntax checks.

Callback: Directly operationalizes the bio-inspired paradox from Slide 11.
Bridge: Cognitive cost is only half the picture—there is also a physical cost behind every query.

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
Beyond Cognition: Material & Ecological Footprint
A brief factual check on the infrastructure behind large-scale AI workflows:



Energy & Resource Rebound

Net \(\text{CO}_2\) Rebound: Global energy–economy modelling indicates that AI-driven productivity gains can enable more \(\text{CO}_2\) emissions than they avoid (Alpine et al., 2026).
Local Water Competition: Rapid data-center expansion concentrates in regions with unresolved water-access pressures—for example, Uruguay (1.77) and Chile (3.49) data centers per 1 million inhabitants (IFC, 2026).
Takeaway for Scientists: Proportionality matters—do not deploy heavy generative or deep-learning compute where a lightweight statistical model already answers the question.








“Only a tiny proportion of water in Uruguay is used for human consumption.” — Daniel Pena, University of the Republic (Rest of World, 2026)




Alpine et al. (2026) npj Clim. Action 5, 71 10.1038/s44168-026-00411-0 · International Finance Corporation (IFC, 2026) · Rest of World (2026)



Spoken core (1 min — sober, factual tone): Keep this grounded and non-alarmist. Beyond cognition, AI has a real physical footprint: global models suggest rebound effects can raise net emissions (Alpine et al., 2026), and data-center placement increasingly intersects with local water stress, as seen in South America (Uruguay at 1.77 and Chile at 3.49 data centers per million inhabitants). As environmental scientists, proportionality is simply good practice.
Callback: Completes Insight 1 (both 1a taxonomy and 1b cognitive + material guardrails).
Bridge: Now that we know what sits under the AI umbrella—and the cognitive and material costs of using it blindly—how do we decide when a scientific problem genuinely justifies moving beyond classical statistics?

title: Let's Talk About AI
section: When Does a Research Problem Need AI?
text:
When Does a Research Problem Need AI?
Scenario: Monitoring 100 river sites to explain or predict species richness across temperature, water chemistry, pollutants, and community variables.



What Is a “Dimension”?

In Ecology / Env. Science: Usually 3D physical space \((x, y, z)\) + time.
In Data Science / ML: Every measured river variable is an axis (\(d\)). Recording 50 chemistry, land-use, and species variables places each river site in a 50-dimensional space.



Scaling the River Study (\(n = 100\) sites)


1DTemp


→


3D+ pH, O2


→


50D+ Chemicals, Land Use & Species


Keeping \(n = 100\) sites fixed while adding axes makes the space exponentially sparse: straight-line Euclidean distances flatten, nearest neighbors stop being truly similar, and classical models run out of degrees of freedom.






In high \(d\), sites often lie on a curved lower-dimensional manifold; straight-line Euclidean distances (white lines) fail to identify truly similar sites.



The Methodological Filter — Matching the Toolkit to the River Study

Stage 1 (1D–3D, known mechanism): Exhaust classical statistics first (Correlation, GLMs).
Stage 2 (50D non-linear tabular data): Dimensionality reduction (PCA/UMAP) + Machine Learning (where my PhD fits).
Stage 3 (Adding satellite imagery/audio or strict sampling constraints): Deep Learning or Symbolic AI.






Spoken core (2 clicks):

Initial state: Anchor the room on one concrete running example—100 river sites where our target is species richness—and clarify the word “dimension” (3D space + time in ecology vs. one axis per measured variable in data science).
Click 1 (Scaling 1D→50D + Swiss Roll visual): As we expand the same 100 sites from temperature alone to 50 chemical, land-use, and species variables, the space becomes exponentially empty. Point to the Swiss Roll: sites that look close along a straight-line white chord are actually far apart along the true ecological manifold.
Click 2 (Methodological Filter): Walk through the 3 stages spanning the full AI umbrella—Stage 1 stays in classical stats, Stage 2 motivates tabular ML (explicitly flagging that my PhD sits here), and Stage 3 justifies Deep Learning or Symbolic AI.

Callback: Connects directly to Slide 12’s expertise thought experiment—domain framing comes first, then this filter checks whether AI is warranted.
Bridge: Now suppose our river study genuinely hits Stage 2 (50 variables, non-linear thresholds). What actually changes under the hood when we step into Machine Learning?

title: Let's Talk About AI
section: Scaling the River Study: From Classical Stats to ML
text:
Scaling the River Study: From Classical Stats to ML
Suppose our 100 river sites reach Stage 2 (50 variables, non-linear thresholds). What actually changes when stepping into ML?



Stage 1: Classical Baseline
\[\text{Richness} = a \cdot \text{Temp} + b + \varepsilon\]
1–3 predictors, solved analytically via OLS/GLM; slope \(a\) carries a direct biological meaning.




→




Stage 2: Same Study Framed as Machine Learning
\[\text{Richness} \sim f(\text{50 chemical, climate \& land-use features})\]
Framed via 3 ML building blocks: (1) Model (algorithm), (2) Loss Function (MSE for continuous richness; Cross-Entropy if classifying ecological status), and (3) Solver (iterative optimization, e.g., gradient descent).
As non-linearity or complexity grows, step deliberately along the toolkit \(\rightarrow\) Trees \(\rightarrow\) Random Forests \(\rightarrow\) SVMs \(\rightarrow\) Neural Nets.






Classical Statistics Dictionary


Machine Learning Dictionary




Covariates / Explanatory variables (X)


Features / Inputs




Response variable (Y) & Residuals


Target / Label & Loss Function




Mechanistic / Biological parameters


Weights / Hyperparameters




Key difference: ML weights optimize prediction and rarely carry direct biological meaning. Exhaust classical exploratory statistics first before scaling up.



Spoken core (2 clicks):

Initial state: Stay on the same 100-river-site richness study. In Stage 1 (1–3 predictors), OLS/GLM gives an exact analytical solution and a biologically interpretable slope \(a\). Walk briefly down the left-to-right translation dictionary below so biostatistics users recognize the parallel terms.
Click 1 (Stage 2 ML framing): At 50 non-linear features, ML is not magic—it simply reformulates the same richness target into three components: Model, Loss Function (MSE for continuous richness, Cross-Entropy for ecological status classes), and Solver, stepping deliberately along the toolkit as needed.
Click 2 (Red key difference bar): Highlight the core scientific caveat—unlike slope \(a\), ML weights optimize prediction and rarely have direct biological meaning, which is why exhausting classical EDA comes first.

Callback: Directly continues the river scenario from Slide 15 and maps onto the toolkit hierarchy from Slide 10.
Bridge: Now let’s pause for two minutes and apply this exact framing to a research question from your own work.

title: Let's Talk About AI
section: The Two Cultures & The Flexible Trade-Off
text:
The Two Cultures & The Flexible Trade-Off



Data Modeling Culture (Classical Statistics)

Assumes data arise from a specified stochastic/mechanistic process (e.g., GLMMs, ODEs).
Primary goal: Parameter inference, uncertainty quantification, and causal interpretation.





↔︎




Algorithmic Modeling Culture (Machine Learning)

Treats the underlying data-generating mechanism as unknown or too complex to write analytically.
Primary goal: Out-of-sample predictive accuracy across high-dimensional, non-linear interactions.







White Box · High Interpretability
River GLM (Y = β0 + β1Temp)  |  GUTS ODEs (kd, z, bw)
Transparent mechanism → directly defensible in regulation.


Grey Box · Interpretable ML & XAI
Decision Trees · Random Forests + Feature Importance
50 river variables → captures non-linearities while auditing key drivers.


Black Box · High Predictive Capacity
Deep Neural Nets (ŷ = fθ(X) on river satellite/acoustic data)
Higher accuracy on complex inputs, opaque → harder to justify in regulation.




A Pragmatic, Objective-Driven Choice: Interpretability is not a dogma—it is an explicit scientific decision. High-throughput screening (e.g., QSARs) may justify prioritizing accuracy; regulatory or mechanistic risk assessment demands explainability. Increasingly, hybrid pipelines combine both.


Breiman, L. (2001). Statistical modeling: The two cultures. Statistical Science, 16(3), 199–231. 10.1214/ss/1009213726 · Rudin, C. (2019). Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead. Nature Machine Intelligence, 1, 206–215. 10.1038/s42256-019-0048-x



Spoken core (2 clicks):

Initial state: Contrast Breiman’s two cultures—Data Modeling (explicit stochastic/mechanistic assumptions for inference) versus Algorithmic Modeling (treating the mechanism as unknown to maximize out-of-sample predictive accuracy).
Click 1 (3-column Spectrum Bar): Map our exact river study across the continuum alongside ecotoxicology: Stage 1’s River GLM and mechanistic GUTS ODEs sit in the White Box (transparent, directly defensible in regulation); Stage 2’s 50-variable Random Forest sits in the Grey Box (capturing non-linearities while auditing drivers); Stage 3’s Deep Neural Nets on satellite or acoustic river streams sit in the Black Box (high accuracy, harder to defend to regulators).
Click 2 (Bottom Blue Box): Emphasize pragmatism—interpretability is an objective-driven choice, not dogma. Connect directly to my PhD: because regulatory ecotoxicology requires mechanistic justification, my work deliberately operates in the White/Grey Box zone (GUTS + interpretable ML) rather than jumping to opaque Deep Learning.

Callback: Unifies the 3-stage river example (Slides 15–16) with the audience’s inference-vs-prediction choices (Slide 17).

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
Take-Home Messages




AI is an Umbrella Toolkit: Map the taxonomy before choosing an algorithm—GenAI chatbots are only one narrow subset.


Protect Cognitive Friction & Proportionality: Preserve your scientific savoir-faire and weigh the ecological footprint of heavy AI workflows.


Earn Model Complexity: Check true dimensionality and exhaust classical statistical analyses before adopting ML.


Align the Trade-Off to Your Goal: Use domain knowledge to decide where interpretability is essential, where predictive power wins, or where hybrid pipelines bridge both.

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
Why ML in My Project?

Positioning this case study along Part 1’s modelling spectrum: coupling a mechanistic core with an interpretable audit.



White Box · High Interpretability
Mechanistic Core: GUTS & DR
Explicit toxicokinetic–toxicodynamic equations calibrated on survival data.


CURRENT FOCUS Grey Box · Interpretable ML & XAI
Towards Explainable ML Audit
Random Forest + %IncMSE auditing how experimental design features govern parameter uncertainty.


Black Box · High Predictive Capacity
Deep Learning / Neural Networks
Deliberately not used in this sample regime and regulatory context.





1. Tabular Data Regime (\(n = 216\))
Tree ensembles limit overfitting compared to deep architectures.


2. Regulatory Traceability (EFSA / OECD)
Auditable links between experimental inputs and parameter uncertainty.


3. Protocol Design Objective
Guiding laboratory study designs, not black-box prediction.




Frame this slide directly as a continuation of Part 1’s spectrum (Slide 19). Remind the audience that Random Forest is already an interpretable ML method used here strictly as an exploratory audit—not yet a final predictive optimizer. Keep the rationale against Deep Learning grounded on objective scientific criteria (moderate tabular n = 216 + regulatory traceability under EFSA/OECD), and explicitly invite the bioinformatics/AI team to challenge this modelling choice during the closing discussion.

title: Let's Talk About AI
section: From Everyday Products to Freshwater Exposure
text:
From Everyday Products to Freshwater Exposure

Regulatory context for non-ecotoxicologists: tracing everyday agricultural products to freshwater screening.



1. Everyday Products
🍎   🍷   🥖
Apple, red wine, and baguette represent routine food chains sustained by intensive crop production.


→


2. Large-Scale Agriculture
🌾   🚜   🧴
Relies on Plant Protection Products (PPPs) to protect yields against fungi, insects, and weeds.


→

Insight 3 from Part 1 in action: exhaust classical statistical methods before invoking non-linear Machine Learning.



1. Descriptive
Compute precision metrics (CV, PUI) and visualise them across design features.
Metrics

CV: Individual parameter uncertainty.
PUI (Bauer et al., 2024): Global parameter precision.



2. Univariate
Test 1-vs-1 monotonic relationships between design features and precision.
Method

Spearman coefficient across experimental design features and precision metrics.



3. Multivariate
Quantify how much variance is captured by linear multivariate combinations.
Method

Redundancy Analysis (RDA) relating design features to precision metrics.



4. ML Audit
Capture non-linear relationships and feature interactions.
Method

Random Forest (\(Y \sim X\)) predicting precision metrics from design features.




This four-step ladder operationalises Insight 3 from Part 1: we do not jump straight to ML. We systematically document what descriptive summaries, rank correlations (Spearman), and linear multivariate models (RDA) can and cannot explain before invoking Random Forests.

Steps 2 & 3 (Univariate & Multivariate): Hitting the Linear Ceiling

Tracking \(\mathcal{D} = \{\mathcal{E}, \mathbf{N}\}\) · Auditing \(Y(\theta) \sim X(\mathcal{E})\)





Spearman correlations: Distinct, weak, or scattered signals across individual parameters and experimental design features.
Redundancy Analysis (RDA): Linear multivariate modelling explains a maximum of ~25% of total variance across models.



Classical linear tools are exhausted \(\rightarrow\) empirically justifying non-linear ML.







Point out that Spearman correlations reveal isolated parameter-specific trends, while Redundancy Analysis tops out at roughly 25% of explained variance. That empirical ceiling—not novelty—is what justifies stepping into Random Forests.

title: Let's Talk About AI
section: Step 4 (ML Audit): Random Forest Feature Importance (%IncMSE)
text:
Step 4 (ML Audit): Random Forest Feature Importance (%IncMSE)

Tracking \(\mathcal{D} = \{\mathcal{E}, \mathbf{N}\}\) · Auditing \(Y(\theta) \sim X(\mathcal{E})\)




\[\%\text{IncMSE} = \frac{\text{MSE}_{\text{permuted}} - \text{MSE}_{\text{base}}}{\text{MSE}_{\text{base}}} \times 100\]


%IncMSE (Percentage Increase in Mean Squared Error) is a feature importance metric: a high value means Random Forest predictions of parameter precision became less accurate when that design feature was randomly permuted.



Maximum Mortality Delta and Number of time points are almost equally relevant across all three models.
DR precision is heavily driven by capturing Partial Effect Concentrations.



Model sanity check (OOB \(R^2\) on global PUI, \(n = 112\text{--}114\)): GUTS-IT: 68.4% | DR: 40.6% | GUTS-SD: 24.5% (Confirms real non-linear signal behind %IncMSE on PUI; individual cv_* ratios exhibit numerical instability near \(\log_{10}(\theta)\approx 0\).)







Be explicit about two methodological safeguards: 1. %IncMSE stands for Percentage Increase in Mean Squared Error and is a permutation-based feature importance metric, NOT a standalone accuracy metric. 2. Before interpreting %IncMSE rankings, we audited Out-Of-Bag (OOB) predictive performance so we do not interpret noise. On the global precision index (PUI), OOB R-squared reaches 68.4% for GUTS-IT, 40.6% for DR, and 24.5% for GUTS-SD (n = 112–114), confirming genuine signal. 3. Auditing OOB R-squared on individual parameter CVs also caught a mathematical artifact: dividing log10 interval width by |log10(median)| explodes whenever a parameter median is close to 1 (log10 ≈ 0), producing extreme outliers (up to 316x the median) and negative OOB R-squared. For the next iteration, individual parameters will use direct log10 widths or GoK instead of this ratio.

Applying the Insight: Why Historical Data Are Not Enough

Tracking \(\mathcal{D} = \{\mathcal{E}, \mathbf{N}\}\) · Auditing \(Y(\theta) \sim X(\mathcal{E})\)




Recap from ML Audit
Maximum Mortality Delta and Number of time points co-drive parameter precision across models.


Structural Limitations of Retrospective Data

Historical datasets leave large gaps in the experimental design space (heavily biased toward legacy OECD protocols).
The relationship is non-linear and multidimensional—we cannot yet extract robust numeric thresholds.
Open regulatory question: If a laboratory design inflates parameter uncertainty (high PUI), how severely does it degrade the final \(LC_{50}\)?








Use the response surface on the right to illustrate sampling sparsity: because historical studies cluster around legacy OECD protocols, large regions of the design space remain empty. Retrospective ML tells us which variables matter, but cannot safely extrapolate thresholds into untested protocol designs. Now step back to formalise the full two-stage architecture we just ran—and how we plan to extend it.

Longer-Term Thesis Horizon

title: Let's Talk About AI
text:
Take-Home Messages




The Legacy Mismatch: Standardised OECD experimental designs are not optimised for dynamic mechanistic models like GUTS.


Structured, Explainable Audit: Separating \(\mathcal{D} = \{\mathcal{E}, \mathbf{N}\}\) inside a two-stage White/Grey Box audit—only after exhausting classical statistics—preserves regulatory auditability.


Audit Before Simulation: Retrospective ML shows what drives precision and exposes historical design gaps, bridging directly to targeted prospective simulation.

section: Open Methodological Challenges: Ecotox \(\leftrightarrow\) AI/Bioinformatics Discussion
text:
Open Methodological Challenges: Ecotox \(\leftrightarrow\) AI/Bioinformatics Discussion

Moving from our Proof-of-Concept to the extended Stage 1 + Stage 2 pipeline and prospective simulation—your input is welcome.



1. Multi-Response Learning
Expanding Stage 1 to jointly include Precision (CV, PUI, GoK), Goodness-of-Fit (GoF), and Predictive Capacity yields correlated targets \(Y(\theta)\).
With \(n \approx 200\) and collinear design features \(X(\mathcal{E})\), should we move to multi-output algorithms (e.g., Multivariate Random Forests) or keep separate single-target models?


2. Leakage-Free Data Splitting
To evaluate GUTS Predictive Capacity on unseen datasets without data leakage across shared species, substances, or source studies:
How should we design grouped / stratified splits on an unbalanced ecotoxicological database?


3. Coupling Meta-Models with Iterative Active Learning
(Building on Baudrot & Charles, 2018)
How can our Stage 2 xAI meta-model serve as a fast surrogate inside an iterative experimental design loop (\(\arg\max D_{KL}\) / Bayesian Optimization) under hard 3Rs and budget constraints?



Leave this slide on screen for the 15-minute open discussion. Prompt both groups specifically: - Question 1 (AI / Stats): Trade-offs between Multivariate RF / multi-task models vs. separate single-output RFs when n ~ 200 and Stage 1 targets (Precision, GoF, Predictive Capacity) are correlated. Also ask about handling collinearity in permutation importance (conditional permutation importance or SHAP) and whether alternative learners should challenge Random Forest here. - Question 2 (Ecotox + AI): What defines a genuinely independent test split—holding out a study, a substance, or a species–substance pair—without collapsing sample size in sparse taxa? - Question 3 (AI + Ecotox): Connecting our Stage 2 surrogate directly to Baudrot & Charles (2018)’s iterative active learning framework (maximising KL divergence) or Bayesian Optimization under hard 3Rs constraints.
